claim: DNA methylation has evolved to silence mutagenic transposable elements (TEs) while typically avoiding the targeting of endogenous genes.
source: DNA methylation has evolved to silence mutagenic transposable elements (TEs) while typically avoiding the targeting of endogenous genes.
evidence: This is a general statement about DNA methylation function supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: microRNA-mediated repression of CHROMOMETHYLASE 3 (CMT3) and the chromatin features that CMT3 prefers help prevent ectopic methylation of thousands of genes during embryogenesis that can persist for weeks afterwards.
source: Here, we report that microRNA-mediated repression of CHROMOMETHYLASE 3 (CMT3) and the chromatin features that CMT3 prefers help prevent ectopic methylation of thousands of genes during embryogenesis that can persist for weeks afterwards.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including methylation profiling and transgenic experiments.

claim: CMT3-induced ectopic methylation of promoters or bodies of genes undergoing transcriptional activation reduces their expression.
source: Our results are also consistent with CMT3-induced ectopic methylation of promoters or bodies of genes undergoing transcriptional activation reducing their expression.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing correlation between CMT3-induced hypermethylation and reduced expression of genes being activated.

claim: Most TEs in Arabidopsis thaliana are found in pericentromeric regions of the genome to which RNA polymerases have limited access.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis), most TEs are found in pericentromeric regions of the genome to which RNA polymerases have limited access (Arabidopsis Genome Initiative, 2000; Lippman et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: TE-enriched constitutive heterochromatic regions are characterized by high densities of cytosine methylation in symmetric (CG or CHG) and asymmetric (CHH) contexts, as well as histone H3 lysine dimethylation (H3K9me2) and other transcriptionally repressive chromatin marks.
source: These TE-enriched constitutive heterochromatic regions are characterized by high densities of cytosine methylation in symmetric (CG or CHG; H ≠ G) and asymmetric (CHH) contexts, as well as histone H3 lysine dimethylation (H3K9me2) and other transcriptionally repressive chromatin marks (Cokus et al., 2008; Lister et al., 2008; Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Symmetric DNA methylation and H3K9me2 facilitate the stable propagation of silenced states through cell divisions.
source: Symmetric DNA methylation and H3K9me2 also facilitate the stable propagation of silenced states through cell divisions (Jackson et al., 2002; Lindroth et al., 2001; Stroud et al., 2013, Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: METHYLTRANSFERASE 1 (MET1) maintains CG methylation through mitotic and meiotic cell divisions with high fidelity due to VARIANT IN METHYLATION 1/2/3 (VIM1/2/3) proteins that recognize hemi-methylated CG and recruit MET1 to methylate daughter strands.
source: METHYLTRANSFERASE 1 (MET1) maintains CG methylation through mitotic and meiotic cell divisions with high fidelity due to VARIANT IN METHYLATION 1/2/3 (VIM1/2/3) proteins that recognize hemi-methylated CG and recruit MET1 to methylate daughter strands (Feng et al., 2010; Finnegan and Dennis, 1993; Ning et al., 2020; Woo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CG methylation can recruit RNA Polymerase IV complexes required to produce 24-nt small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) that are then loaded onto Argonaute proteins and guide them to target loci by base-pairing with nucleic acids.
source: CG methylation can also recruit RNA Polymerase IV complexes required to produce 24-nt small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) that are then loaded onto Argonaute proteins and guide them to target loci by base-pairing with nucleic acids (Blevins et al., 2015; Herr et al., 2005; Papareddy et al., 2020; Zhai et al., 2015; Zilberman, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM) leads to the recruitment of DOMAINS REARRANGED METHYLTRANSFERASES 1/2 (DRM1/2) and results in de novo methylation of cytosines in all sequence contexts, including CHH.
source: This leads to the recruitment of DOMAINS REARRANGED METHYLTRANSFERASES 1/2 (DRM1/2) and results in de novo methylation of cytosines in all sequence contexts, including CHH, which is a hallmark feature of RNA-directed DNA methylation (RdDM) (Cao and Jacobsen, 2002; Stroud et al., 2013; Wierzbicki et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RdDM is typically restricted from constitutive heterochromatin because it is inaccessible to DNA-dependent RNA polymerase IV and methyltransferases required for RdDM.
source: However, RdDM is typically restricted from constitutive heterochromatin because it is inaccessible to DNA-dependent RNA polymerase IV and methyltransferases required for RdDM (Papareddy et al., 2020; Zemach et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CHH methylation of constitutive heterochromatin is mediated by CHROMOMETHYLASE 2 (CMT2) that binds to H3K9me2 deposited by KRYPTONITE (KYP) and closely related SUPPRESSOR OF VARIEGATION 3–9 HOMOLOGUE PROTEIN 5/6 (SUVH5/6) methyltransferases.
source: Instead, CHH methylation of constitutive heterochromatin is mediated by CHROMOMETHYLASE 2 (CMT2) that binds to H3K9me2 deposited by KRYPTONITE (KYP) and closely related SUPPRESSOR OF VARIEGATION 3–9 HOMOLOGUE PROTEIN 5/6 (SUVH5/6) methyltransferases (Stroud et al., 2014; Zemach et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CHROMOMETHYLASE 3 (CMT3) forms interlocking positive feedback loops with H3K9 methyltransferases.
source: CHROMOMETHYLASE 3 (CMT3) also forms interlocking positive feedback loops with H3K9 methyltransferases (Du et al., 2012; Jackson et al., 2002; Lindroth et al., 2001) but is more closely associated with the cell cycle and mediates CHG methylation (Ning et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CMT3 is more closely associated with the cell cycle and mediates CHG methylation.
source: CHROMOMETHYLASE 3 (CMT3) also forms interlocking positive feedback loops with H3K9 methyltransferases (Du et al., 2012; Jackson et al., 2002; Lindroth et al., 2001) but is more closely associated with the cell cycle and mediates CHG methylation (Ning et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CMT3-mediated CHG methylation is largely deposited on TEs.
source: CMT3-mediated CHG methylation is largely deposited on TEs.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: CMT3 can induce the ectopic methylation of protein-coding genes.
source: However, CMT3 can also induce the ectopic methylation of protein-coding genes (Wendte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The introduction of Arabidopsis CMT3 transgenes into Eutrema salsugineum, which lost CMT3 millions of years ago, could occasionally reconstitute CG methylation on genes.
source: Moreover, the introduction of Arabidopsis CMT3 transgenes into Eutrema salsugineum, which lost CMT3 millions of years ago (Bewick et al., 2016), could occasionally reconstitute CG methylation on genes (Wendte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CMT3-induced gene-body methylation (gbM) could be stably maintained independent of the CMT3 transgene for several generations.
source: The resulting gene-body methylation (gbM) could be stably maintained independent of the CMT3 transgene for several generations (Wendte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Methylated cytosines are mutagenic due to associated cytosine deamination.
source: Because methylated cytosines are mutagenic due to associated cytosine deamination (Shen et al., 1992; Sved and Bird, 1990), features associated with gbM have been interpreted as evidence that gbM provides selective advantages that counterbalance this mutagenesis-imposed fitness penalty.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: gbM is depleted from transcription start and end sites.
source: For instance, gbM is depleted from transcription start and end sites (Tran et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2006; Zilberman et al., 2007), and it has recently been reported that gbM helps prevent transcription initiation from cryptic promoters located in gene bodies as initially proposed (Choi et al., 2020; Zilberman et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: gbM helps prevent transcription initiation from cryptic promoters located in gene bodies.
source: For instance, gbM is depleted from transcription start and end sites (Tran et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2006; Zilberman et al., 2007), and it has recently been reported that gbM helps prevent transcription initiation from cryptic promoters located in gene bodies as initially proposed (Choi et al., 2020; Zilberman et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: gbM tends to be enriched on constitutively expressed genes.
source: Moreover, gbM tends to be enriched on constitutively expressed genes (Lister et al., 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2016; Takuno et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2006), which would be consistent with gbM stabilizing gene expression by excluding certain histone variants (i.e. H2A.Z) from genes (Coleman-Derr and Zilberman, 2012) and generally enhancing gene expression (Muyle and Gaut, 2019; Shahzad et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: gbM may stabilize gene expression by excluding certain histone variants (i.e. H2A.Z) from genes.
source: Moreover, gbM tends to be enriched on constitutively expressed genes (Lister et al., 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2016; Takuno et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2006), which would be consistent with gbM stabilizing gene expression by excluding certain histone variants (i.e. H2A.Z) from genes (Coleman-Derr and Zilberman, 2012) and generally enhancing gene expression (Muyle and Gaut, 2019; Shahzad et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from cited studies.

claim: Accumulating evidence is consistent with gbM being a heritable by-product of CMT3-induced epimutations.
source: Nevertheless, accumulating evidence is also consistent with gbM being a heritable by-product of CMT3-induced epimutations (Bewick et al., 2016; Bewick et al., 2019; Wendte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mechanisms exist that transcriptionally and post-translationally regulate CMT3.
source: Consistent with the need to fine-tune the amount of CMT3 activities required to both silence TEs and prevent epimutations on genes, mechanisms exist that transcriptionally (Ning et al., 2020) and post-translationally (Deng et al., 2016) regulate CMT3, as well as remove H3K9me2 specifically from expressed genes (Inagaki et al., 2010; Saze et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MET1 and VIM1/2/3 are required for the faithful transmission of mCG across cell cycles.
source: MET1 and VIM1/2/3 are required for the faithful transmission of mCG across cell cycles (Feng et al., 2010; Finnegan and Dennis, 1993; Ning et al., 2020; Woo et al., 2008) and accordingly had increased transcript levels in rapidly dividing early embryos that also correlated well with transcripts encoding cell-cycle activators throughout embryogenesis (Figure 1A; Hofmann et al., 2019; Papareddy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MET1 and VIM1/2/3 had increased transcript levels in rapidly dividing early embryos that also correlated well with transcripts encoding cell-cycle activators throughout embryogenesis.
source: MET1 and VIM1/2/3 are required for the faithful transmission of mCG across cell cycles (Feng et al., 2010; Finnegan and Dennis, 1993; Ning et al., 2020; Woo et al., 2008) and accordingly had increased transcript levels in rapidly dividing early embryos that also correlated well with transcripts encoding cell-cycle activators throughout embryogenesis (Figure 1A; Hofmann et al., 2019; Papareddy et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and citations.

claim: MET1 and VIM1/2/3 transcript levels peaked at the early heart stage and were reduced afterwards before plummeting at the mature green stage.
source: More specifically, MET1 and VIM1/2/3 transcript levels peaked at the early heart stage and were reduced afterwards before plummeting at the mature green stage.
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transcript developmental dynamics of MET1 and VIM1/2/3 were characteristic of transcripts encoding proteins involved in licensing DNA replication, heterochromatin maintenance and DNA methylation, but not randomized controls.
source: These transcript developmental dynamics were also characteristic of transcripts encoding proteins involved in licensing DNA replication (e.g. Cyclins A2/B1, CDKB1-1, MINICHROMOSOME MAINTENANCE2), heterochromatin maintenance (e.g. DDM1) and DNA methylation (e.g. CMT3), but not randomized controls (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Genes required for DNA methylation and heterochromatin maintenance are tightly correlated with cell-cycle activity during embryogenesis.
source: Therefore, genes required for DNA methylation and heterochromatin maintenance are tightly correlated with cell-cycle activity during embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 70% of differentially methylated cytosines (DMCs) occurred in the CHH context.
source: Similar to previous observations (Bouyer et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2017; Papareddy et al., 2020), 70% of DMCs occurred in the CHH context (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and citations to previous studies.

claim: Substantial fractions of DMCs occurred in CG (20%) or CHG (10%) contexts.
source: Consistent with dynamic expression patterns of MET1 and CMT3, substantial fractions of DMCs occurred in CG (20%) or CHG (10%) contexts, respectively.
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript.

claim: DNA methylation is dynamically reconfigured in all sequence contexts during embryogenesis.
source: Therefore, DNA methylation is dynamically reconfigured in all sequence contexts during embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Symmetric DMCs represented 1185 CG and 1398 CHG differentially methylated regions (DMRs) covering 201 kb and 185.8 kb, respectively.
source: In total, these symmetric DMCs represented 1185 CG (Supplementary file 1) and 1398 CHG (Supplementary file 2) differentially methylated regions (DMRs) covering 201 kb and 185.8 kb, respectively (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and supplementary files.

claim: A significant fraction of CG and CHG DMRs overlapped (n = 183; 7.1% of total).
source: Although a significant fraction of CG and CHG DMRs overlapped (n = 183; 7.1% of total), the vast majority of CG and CHG DMRs were located in non-overlapping genomic regions corresponding to euchromatic gene-rich and heterochromatic TE-rich regions of the genome, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The vast majority of CG and CHG DMRs were located in non-overlapping genomic regions corresponding to euchromatic gene-rich and heterochromatic TE-rich regions of the genome, respectively.
source: Although a significant fraction of CG and CHG DMRs overlapped (n = 183; 7.1% of total), the vast majority of CG and CHG DMRs were located in non-overlapping genomic regions corresponding to euchromatic gene-rich and heterochromatic TE-rich regions of the genome, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Leaves deficient in CG methylation did not have reduced CHG methylation in CHG DMRs regardless of whether or not they overlapped with CG DMRs.
source: Leaves deficient in CG methylation did not have reduced CHG methylation in CHG DMRs regardless of whether or not they overlapped with CG DMRs (Figure 1E,F; data from Stroud et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E,F from a previous study.

claim: CHG DMRs occur in distinct genomic regions and are largely independent of CG methylation.
source: This indicates that CHG DMRs occur in distinct genomic regions and are largely independent of CG methylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Relative to floral bud samples, CG DMRs have slightly reduced methylation in preglobular embryos, followed by increased methylation until after the torpedo stage, when levels dramatically reduce in mature green embryos and recover in leaves.
source: Relative to floral bud samples, CG DMRs have slightly reduced methylation in preglobular embryos, followed by increased methylation until after the torpedo stage, when levels dramatically reduce in mature green embryos and recover in leaves (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Methylation levels of CHG DMRs are relatively stable between floral buds and early embryos, then decrease in late embryos, reaching a minimum in leaves.
source: By contrast, methylation levels of CHG DMRs are relatively stable between floral buds and early embryos, then decrease in late embryos, reaching a minimum in leaves (Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Changes in CG and CHG DMR methylation levels during development were significantly correlated with MET1 (Pearson's R = 0.8; p value = 0.03) and CMT3 (Pearson's R = 0.74; p value = 0.05) transcript levels, respectively.
source: Accordingly, changes in CG and CHG DMR methylation levels during development were significantly correlated with MET1 (Pearson's R = 0.8; p value = 0.03) and CMT3 (Pearson's R = 0.74; p value = 0.05) transcript levels, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Distinct mechanisms reconfigure CG or CHG methylation genome-wide during embryogenesis.
source: Therefore, although cell division rates are correlated with symmetric DNA methylation dynamics, distinct mechanisms reconfigure CG or CHG methylation genome-wide during embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CG methylation on both euchromatic and heterochromatic TEs was slightly reduced in pregobular embryos and then restored to the levels found in floral buds by the early heart stage.
source: CG methylation on both euchromatic and heterochromatic TEs was slightly reduced in pregobular embryos and then restored to the levels found in floral buds by the early heart stage (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: CG methylation of euchromatic TEs was relatively constant for the remainder of embryogenesis, whereas heterochromatic TEs had significantly increased methylation during late embryogenesis compared to post-embryonic tissues.
source: Whereas CG methylation of euchromatic TEs was relatively constant for the remainder of embryogenesis, heterochromatic TEs had significantly increased methylation during late embryogenesis compared to post-embryonic tissues.
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CG hypermethylation in mature green compared to bent cotyledon embryos predominantly occurred in pericentromeric genomic regions rather than gene-rich chromosomal arms.
source: Consistent with heterochromatin becoming highly condensed during embryo maturation (van Zanten et al., 2011), we found that CG hypermethylation in mature green compared to bent cotyledon embryos predominantly occurred in pericentromeric genomic regions rather than gene-rich chromosomal arms (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and a citation.

claim: CG methylation was required for the production of 24-nt siRNAs from euchromatic TEs, but only marginally for heterochromatic TEs.
source: CG methylation was required for the production of 24-nt siRNAs from euchromatic TEs, but only marginally for heterochromatic TEs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, data from Lister et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A from a previous study.

claim: The loss of 24-nt siRNAs in nrpd1a mutants only had negligible effects on CG methylation of both heterochromatic and euchromatic TEs.
source: Conversely, the loss of 24-nt siRNAs in nrpd1a mutants only had negligible effects on CG methylation of both heterochromatic and euchromatic TEs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: siRNA production from euchromatic regions of the genome requires CG methylation, but not vice versa.
source: Therefore, siRNA production from euchromatic regions of the genome requires CG methylation, but not vice versa.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Global CHG methylation of euchromatic and heterochromatic TEs was higher in embryos compared to leaves.
source: Global CHG methylation of euchromatic and heterochromatic TEs was higher in embryos compared to leaves (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: siRNA-deficient nrpd1a mutant tissues had reduced CHG methylation on euchromatic or heterochromatic TEs in all or only embryonic samples, respectively.
source: Similar to previous observations for CHH methylation (Papareddy et al., 2020), siRNA-deficient nrpd1a mutant tissues had reduced CHG methylation on euchromatic or heterochromatic TEs in all or only embryonic samples, respectively (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F,G and a citation.

claim: Increased CHH methylation on heterochromatic TEs was significantly correlated with decreased CHG methylation during late stages of embryogenesis when cell division rates are reduced.
source: Intriguingly, increased CHH methylation on heterochromatic TEs was significantly correlated with decreased CHG methylation during late stages of embryogenesis when cell division rates are reduced (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: CMT3-dependent CHG and CMT2-dependent CHH methylation of heterochromatic TEs are positively and negatively correlated with cell division rates, respectively.
source: Therefore, CMT3-dependent CHG and CMT2-dependent CHH methylation of heterochromatic TEs are positively and negatively correlated with cell division rates, respectively.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CMT3 is recruited to loci by binding to H3K9me2 deposited by SUVH4/5/6 histone methyltransferases.
source: CMT3 is recruited to loci by binding to H3K9me2 deposited by SUVH4/5/6 histone methyltransferases (Du et al., 2012; Jackson et al., 2002; Lindroth et al., 2001; Stroud et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CMT3 and KYP were dynamically expressed according to patterns characteristic of other cell-cycle regulated genes and CHG methylation dynamics.
source: CMT3 and KYP, which is the major SUVH4 H3K9 methyltransferase, were dynamically expressed according to patterns characteristic of other cell-cycle regulated genes and CHG methylation dynamics (Figure 1B,H, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B,H, Figure 3A.

claim: CMT3 and KYP were highly expressed in rapidly dividing early embryos and had reduced expression in late embryos until the mature stage, where they were barely detectable.
source: More specifically, CMT3 and KYP were highly expressed in rapidly dividing early embryos and had reduced expression in late embryos until the mature stage, where they were barely detectable.
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The more rapid cell divisions in early embryos demand higher levels of CMT3 and KYP to maintain mCHG through the cell cycle.
source: Altogether, our results are consistent with the idea that the more rapid cell divisions in early embryos demand higher levels of CMT3 and KYP to maintain mCHG through the cell cycle.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IBM1 is dynamically expressed during embryogenesis in a pattern that strongly resembles CMT3 and KYP.
source: Moreover, IBM1, which encodes an H3K9me2 demethylase and prevents CMT3 recruitment to gene bodies (Miura et al., 2009; Saze et al., 2008), is dynamically expressed during embryogenesis in a pattern that strongly resembles CMT3 and KYP (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citations.

claim: Co-expression of IBM1 with CMT3 and KYP likely helps limit ectopic H3K9me2 and methylated CHG on gene bodies during embryogenesis.
source: Therefore, co-expression of IBM1 with CMT3 and KYP likely helps limit ectopic H3K9me2 and methylated CHG on gene bodies during embryogenesis as has been demonstrated during post-embryonic development (Inagaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data and supported by a citation.

claim: miR823-directed cleavage of CMT3 transcripts is highly enriched in embryos directly after morphogenesis.
source: We previously found that miR823-directed cleavage of CMT3 transcripts is highly enriched in embryos directly after morphogenesis (Plotnikova et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: miR823 accumulates during embryogenesis, and miR823:CMT3 cleavage products were enriched and significantly detected specifically at late heart and early torpedo stages precisely when CMT3 transcript levels were sharply decreasing.
source: In contrast to CMT3 transcript dynamics, miR823 accumulates during embryogenesis, and miR823:CMT3 cleavage products were enriched and significantly detected specifically at late heart and early torpedo stages precisely when CMT3 transcript levels were sharply decreasing (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both independently generated mir823-1 and mir823-2 mutants had significantly increased CMT3 levels relative to wild type in embryos at the bent cotyledon stage when CMT3 levels are normally reduced.
source: Both independently generated mir823-1 and mir823-2 mutants were confirmed as nulls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and had significantly increased CMT3 levels relative to wild type (WT) in embryos at the bent cotyledon stage when CMT3 levels are normally reduced (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: miR823-directed cleavage of CMT3 is highly enriched in embryos.
source: Consistent with miR823-directed cleavage of CMT3 being highly enriched in embryos, we did not observe increased CMT3 transcripts in either leaves or floral buds of mir823 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CHG, but not CG or CHH, methylation was increased on TEs in bent cotyledon embryos of both mir823-1 and mir823-2 mutants relative to WT.
source: Moreover, CHG, but not CG or CHH, methylation was increased on TEs in bent cotyledon embryos of both mir823-1 and mir823-2 mutants relative to WT (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CMT3 transcript levels were increased in rCMT3 relative to cCMT3 lines at the bent cotyledon stage.
source: CMT3 transcript levels were increased in rCMT3 relative to cCMT3 lines at the bent cotyledon stage (Figure 3C), but not in leaves or floral buds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which further indicates that miR823-directed cleavage and repression of CMT3 is highly enriched in embryos transitioning between morphogenesis and maturation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: miR823-directed cleavage and repression of CMT3 is highly enriched in embryos transitioning between morphogenesis and maturation.
source: CMT3 transcript levels were increased in rCMT3 relative to cCMT3 lines at the bent cotyledon stage (Figure 3C), but not in leaves or floral buds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), which further indicates that miR823-directed cleavage and repression of CMT3 is highly enriched in embryos transitioning between morphogenesis and maturation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CMT3 levels were increased in cCMT3 and rCMT3 lines compared to Col-0 in embryos, leaves, and floral buds.
source: CMT3 levels were also increased in cCMT3 and rCMT3 lines compared to Col-0 in embryos, leaves, and floral buds (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) suggesting that miR823 is not sufficient to repress transgenic CMT3 to the same extent as endogenous CMT3 transcripts.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: miR823 is not sufficient to repress transgenic CMT3 to the same extent as endogenous CMT3 transcripts.
source: CMT3 levels were also increased in cCMT3 and rCMT3 lines compared to Col-0 in embryos, leaves, and floral buds (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) suggesting that miR823 is not sufficient to repress transgenic CMT3 to the same extent as endogenous CMT3 transcripts.
evidence: This claim is inferred from data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CMT3 levels are finely tuned during embryogenesis.
source: Nevertheless, it is clear that CMT3 levels are finely tuned during embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: miR823 cleaves and represses CMT3 levels during mid-embryogenesis.
source: Together with the analysis of mir823 mutants and miR823-mediated CMT3 transcript cleavage products (Plotnikova et al., 2019), these results strongly indicate that miR823 cleaves and represses CMT3 levels during mid-embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript and a citation.

claim: Increased CMT3 transcript levels in cCMT3 and rCMT3 embryos resulted in CHG hypermethylation of TEs but did not globally influence CG or CHH methylation.
source: Consistent with what we observed in mir823 mutants, increased CMT3 transcript levels in cCMT3 and rCMT3 embryos resulted in CHG hypermethylation of TEs (Figure 3D) but did not globally influence CG or CHH methylation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: Increased CMT3 transcript levels in mir823 mutants, cCMT3 and most strikingly rCMT3 embryos were associated with ectopic CHG methylation on protein-coding gene bodies and flanking regions in bent cotyledon embryos.
source: Remarkably, increased CMT3 transcript levels in mir823 mutants, cCMT3 and most strikingly rCMT3 embryos were associated with ectopic CHG methylation on protein-coding gene bodies and flanking regions in bent cotyledon embryos (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Both TEs and genes are hypermethylated when CMT3 levels are not properly downregulated upon the morphogenesis-to-maturation transition during embryogenesis.
source: Therefore, both TEs and genes are hypermethylated when CMT3 levels are not properly downregulated upon the morphogenesis-to-maturation transition during embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TEs had increased CHG methylation levels in both cCMT3 lines relative to WT, but protein-coding genes were not affected in 3-week old plants.
source: Although TEs had increased CHG methylation levels in both cCMT3 lines relative to WT, protein-coding genes were not affected (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: TEs and genes were hypermethylated in both rCMT3 lines compared to cCMT3 or WT plants in 3-week old plants, and only slightly reduced relative to the levels observed in rCMT3 bent cotyledon embryos.
source: In stark contrast, TEs and genes were hypermethylated in both rCMT3 lines compared to cCMT3 or WT plants, and only slightly reduced relative to the levels observed in rCMT3 bent cotyledon embryos (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: miR823-directed repression of CMT3 is required to prevent the hypermethylation of protein-coding genes that can be maintained weeks after the completion of embryogenesis.
source: Together with miR823-independent processes (e.g. IBM1 removal of H3K9me2), miR823-directed repression of CMT3 is therefore required to prevent the hypermethylation of protein-coding genes that can be maintained weeks after the completion of embryogenesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CMT3-induced hypermethylation predominantly occurred in the CMT3-preferred CWG context although hypermethylation was also found in CCG and slightly, but significantly in non-CHG contexts, including CG characteristic of gbM.
source: As expected, CMT3-induced hypermethylation predominantly occurred in the CMT3-preferred CWG context (Gouil and Baulcombe, 2016; Li et al., 2018) although hypermethylation was also found in CCG and slightly, but significantly in non-CHG contexts, including CG characteristic of gbM similar to previous observations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H; Wendte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and citations.

claim: CMT3-induced hypermethylation was proportional to patterns of nucleosome occupancy and biased towards the 3' ends of gene bodies, which was highly similar to CG methylation.
source: Consistent with methyltransferases preferring nucleosome-rich DNA as substrates (Chodavarapu et al., 2010; Du et al., 2012), CMT3-induced hypermethylation was proportional to patterns of nucleosome occupancy and biased towards the 3' ends of gene bodies, which was highly similar to CG methylation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I, and citations.

claim: CMT3-induced CHG hypermethylation was proportional to H1 levels across gene bodies.
source: Nucleosome spacing is promoted by linker histone 1 (H1) (Choi et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2003) and CMT3-induced CHG hypermethylation was proportional to H1 levels across gene bodies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1J and citations.

claim: CHG hypermethylation across the four groups was positively correlated with levels of the stable histone variants H2A, H2A.X and most notably H2A.W.
source: Indeed, CHG hypermethylation across the four groups was positively correlated with levels of the stable histone variants H2A, H2A.X and most notably H2A.W that was recently shown to be required for CHG methylation (Figure 4E,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K; Bourguet et al., 2021; Yelagandula et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1K and citations.

claim: CMT3-induced CHG hypermethylation was tightly associated with transcriptionally repressive H3K9me2 marks.
source: CMT3-induced CHG hypermethylation was also tightly associated with transcriptionally repressive H3K9me2 marks, which are required for interdependent feedback loops with CMT3 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: CMT3-induced CHG hypermethylation was inversely related to H2A.Z and marks indicative of active transcription including H3K4me3 and H3K9ac.
source: It was inversely related to H2A.Z (Figure 4H) and marks indicative of active transcription including H3K4me3 and H3K9ac (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H, 4I, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1L.

claim: Genes with CHG hypermethylation had reduced chromatin accessibility and were generally closer to heterochromatic centromeres.
source: Further suggesting that deregulated CMT3 prefers features typically associated with inaccessible chromatin, genes with CHG hypermethylation had reduced chromatin accessibility (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M) and were generally closer to heterochromatic centromeres (Figure 4—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M and 1N.

claim: The most CMT3-induced hypermethylated genes (i.e. cluster 4) were also substantially hypermethylated in ddm1 mutants.
source: Moreover, the most CMT3-induced hypermethylated genes (i.e. cluster 4) were also substantially hypermethylated in ddm1 mutants (Figure 4J) that have increased heterochromatic accessibility (Figure 4K) and decreased stability (Mathieu et al., 2003; Soppe et al., 2002; Zhong et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4J and 4K, and citations.

claim: mCG is not strictly required for ectopic CHG hypermethylation of genes.
source: Although CMT3-induced CHG hypermethylation was strongly associated with CG gene-body methylation (gbM), both the independence of developmental mCHG DMRs (Figure 1E,F) and the gain of mCHG being associated with proportional loss of mCG over genes in ddm1 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1O; Ito et al., 2015; Stroud et al., 2013; Zemach et al., 2013) indicate that mCG is not strictly required for ectopic CHG hypermethylation of genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from data shown in Figure 1E,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1O, and citations.

claim: The associations between chromatin features of genes and their propensity for CMT3-induced hypermethylation suggest that excessive CMT3 is ectopically recruited to genic chromatin characterized by nucleosome stability and inaccessibility.
source: Instead, the associations between chromatin features of genes and their propensity for CMT3-induced hypermethylation altogether suggest that excessive CMT3 is ectopically recruited to genic chromatin characterized by nucleosome stability and inaccessibility.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Differences in global transcript levels were not observed across the four clusters with increasing levels of CMT3-induced CHG methylation.
source: Differences in global transcript levels were not observed across the four clusters with increasing levels of CMT3-induced CHG methylation suggesting that ectopic CHG methylation alone was not sufficient to globally repress gene expression (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 916 genes were differentially expressed between rCMT3 and WT embryos.
source: We then identified 916 genes that were differentially expressed between rCMT3 and WT embryos (i.e. ≥2-fold differences and adj. p values ≤ 0.01; see Materials and methods) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: 87.5% of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) overlapped between rCMT3 line #1 and rCMT3 line #3.
source: Differentially expressed genes (DEGs), defined by comparing either rCMT3 line #1 or rCMT3 line #3 with WT, were commonly detected in both independently generated lines with 87.5% of genes overlapping (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DEGs were less hypermethylated compared to all expressed genes, which indicates that the vast majority of changes in gene expression observed upon up-regulation of CMT3 were not directly due to their hypermethylation.
source: In both rCMT3 lines, DEGs were less hypermethylated compared to all expressed genes, which indicates that the vast majority of changes in gene expression observed upon up-regulation of CMT3 were not directly due to their hypermethylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is inferred from data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 4603 (97% of total) CHG hypermethylated and 127 (3% of total) hypomethylated DMRs were identified in rCMT3 compared to WT bent cotyledon embryos.
source: We then examined whether hypermethylation affects a subset of genes by computing DMRs in rCMT3 compared to WT bent cotyledon embryos and identified 4603 (97% of total) and 127 (3% of total) CHG hypermethylated and hypomethylated DMRs, respectively (Supplementary file 4; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Only a small but significant number of the down-regulated genes overlapped DMRs (21 of 542, 3.8% of total).
source: Further suggesting that CHG hypermethylation has minimal direct consequences on the expression of most genes under the conditions examined, we found that only a small but significant number of the down-regulated genes (including 1.5 kb regions flanking their transcriptional units) overlapped DMRs (21 of 542, 3.8% of total; Fisher's exact test, p value = 1.29e-05) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The DMRs overlapping 21 down-regulated genes were significantly CHG hypermethylated compared to genomic bins.
source: Consistent with CMT3-induced hypermethylation repressing their expression, the DMRs overlapping these 21 down-regulated genes were significantly CHG hypermethylated compared to genomic bins (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The stronger-expressing rCMT3 line #3 had significantly higher CHG methylation compared to rCMT3 line #1.
source: Moreover, the stronger-expressing rCMT3 line #3 had significantly higher CHG methylation compared to rCMT3 line #1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Increased CMT3 levels lead to more ectopic CHG methylation.
source: This further supports that increased CMT3 levels lead to more ectopic CHG methylation (Inagaki et al., 2010; Inagaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data and supported by citations.

claim: Transcripts corresponding to 21 CMT3-induced hypermethylated and down-regulated genes were rapidly increasing when embryos were transitioning to the maturation phase.
source: Strikingly, transcripts corresponding to these 21 CMT3-induced hypermethylated and down-regulated genes were rapidly increasing when embryos were transitioning to the maturation phase (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 10 of 21 CMT3-induced hypermethylated and down-regulated genes were among a group of 381 genes previously identified to be rapidly activated at the morphogenesis-to-maturation transition.
source: Moreover, 10 of these 21 genes (Fisher's exact test, P value = 1.49e-13), were among a group of 381 genes previously identified to also be rapidly activated at these time points (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G; Hofmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and a citation.

claim: Nearly half of 381 rapidly activated genes (n = 183, 48%) were among the 563 significantly down-regulated genes in rCMT3 embryos compared to WT.
source: Nearly half of these 381 genes (n = 183, 48%) were also among the 563 significantly down-regulated genes in rCMT3 embryos compared to WT.
evidence: This claim is based on data presented in the manuscript.

claim: When CMT3 is not properly repressed it can induce ectopic hypermethylation of genes.
source: Altogether, our expression and methylation analyses suggest that when CMT3 is not properly repressed it can induce ectopic hypermethylation of genes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CMT3-induced hypermethylation of gene promoters or bodies can reduce the steady state levels of transcripts from genes that are in the process of switching from silent to active transcriptional states.
source: Furthermore, we suggest that CMT3-induced hypermethylation of gene promoters or bodies can reduce the steady state levels of transcripts from genes that are in the process of switching from silent to active transcriptional states.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: The expression of MET1 and CMT3 methyltransferases and corresponding CG and CHG methylation are intricately linked to mitotic indices through distinct mechanisms.
source: We found that the expression of MET1 and CMT3 methyltransferases and corresponding CG and CHG methylation are intricately linked to mitotic indices through distinct mechanisms (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from data shown in Figure 1.

claim: miR823-mediated cleavage and repression of CMT3 following the proliferative early phase of embryogenesis helps prevent excess CMT3 from ectopically methylating protein-coding genes that can persist for weeks afterwards.
source: Moreover, miR823-mediated cleavage and repression of CMT3 following the proliferative early phase of embryogenesis helps prevent excess CMT3 from ectopically methylating protein-coding genes that can persist for weeks afterwards (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CMT3-induced hypermethylation of genes was highly associated with features conferring nucleosome stability.
source: CMT3-induced hypermethylation of genes was highly associated with features conferring nucleosome stability (Figure 4) and resulted in the repression of genes that are transcriptionally activated (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CMT3-induced hypermethylation of genes resulted in the repression of genes that are transcriptionally activated.
source: CMT3-induced hypermethylation of genes was highly associated with features conferring nucleosome stability (Figure 4) and resulted in the repression of genes that are transcriptionally activated (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Repression of CMT3 following a period when it is needed in high quantity to keep pace with TE methylation prevents CMT3 from ectopically targeting protein-coding genes for methylation.
source: Repression of CMT3 following a period when it is needed in high quantity to keep pace with TE methylation therefore prevents CMT3 from ectopically targeting protein-coding genes for methylation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CMT3-induced epigenetic collateral damage on protein-coding genes appears to negatively affect gene expression.
source: This resulting epigenetic collateral damage on protein-coding genes appears to negatively affect gene expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CMT3-induced epimutations give rise to CG gene-body methylation (gbM) that can be maintained by MET1 across many generations.
source: Our results are consistent with the model that CMT3-induced epimutations give rise to CG gene-body methylation (gbM) that can be maintained by MET1 across many generations (Wendte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data and a citation.

claim: When embryos are transitioning to stages with reduced cell division, decreased CMT3-mediated CHG methylation is correlated with increased CMT2-mediated CHH methylation.
source: CHG and CHH methylation exhibit opposite developmental dynamics depending on the tissue's mitotic index (Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 6; Papareddy et al., 2020). When embryos are transitioning to stages with reduced cell division, decreased CMT3-mediated CHG methylation is correlated with increased CMT2-mediated CHH methylation (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2H and citations.

claim: Handing over TE silencing to CMT2-dependent CHH methylation in cells with reduced division rates likely reduces ectopic methylation of protein-coding genes.
source: Therefore, handing over TE silencing to CMT2-dependent CHH methylation in cells with reduced division rates likely reduces ectopic methylation of protein-coding genes.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: Varying degrees of mitotic indices across development can readily explain the genome-wide patterns of non-CG methylation reported thus far.
source: In addition to what we observed during embryogenesis, varying degrees of mitotic indices across development can readily explain the genome-wide patterns of non-CG methylation reported thus far (Borges et al., 2021; Calarco et al., 2012; Gutzat et al., 2020; Ji et al., 2019; Kawakatsu et al., 2016, Kawakatsu et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2017; Narsai et al., 2017; Papareddy and Nodine, 2021).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data and citations.

claim: Destabilization of heterochromatin in ddm1 mutants redirects CMT3 to genic regions with stable nucleosomes.
source: Therefore, we propose that destabilization of heterochromatin in ddm1 mutants redirects CMT3 to genic regions with stable nucleosomes.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: Factors such as DDM1 that stabilize heterochromatin may be yet another mechanism required to regulate CMT3 activity in order to achieve proper epigenome homeostasis.
source: Therefore, factors such as DDM1 that stabilize heterochromatin may be yet another mechanism required to regulate CMT3 activity in order to achieve proper epigenome homeostasis (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: It is possible that CMT3-induced methylation can form feedback loops with H3K9me2 methyltransferases when genes are transcriptionally inert.
source: Because IBM1-mediated removal of H3K9me2 marks is coupled to transcription (Inagaki et al., 2017), it is possible that CMT3-induced methylation can form feedback loops with H3K9me2 methyltransferases when genes are transcriptionally inert.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data and a citation.

claim: When genes are switched on, H3K9me2 could repress initial rounds of transcription before it is removed by IBM1.
source: However, when genes are switched on, H3K9me2 could repress initial rounds of transcription before it is removed by IBM1.
evidence: This claim is speculative.

claim: Epigenetic collateral damage occurring in embryos may also negatively impact gene expression later in life.
source: Therefore, epigenetic collateral damage occurring in embryos may also negatively impact gene expression later in life.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the data.

claim: Errors in restricting CMT3 to heterochromatin are inevitable on an evolutionary timescale.
source: However, errors in restricting CMT3 to heterochromatin are inevitable on an evolutionary timescale (Zhang et al., 2020) and recent studies indicate that CMT3-induced methylation of genes precedes gbM (Wendte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: CMT3-induced methylation of genes precedes gbM.
source: However, errors in restricting CMT3 to heterochromatin are inevitable on an evolutionary timescale (Zhang et al., 2020) and recent studies indicate that CMT3-induced methylation of genes precedes gbM (Wendte et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: gbM may be merely an evolutionary record of epigenetic collateral damage events that occurred in the past.
source: Because gbM can be stably maintained over many generations by MET1 and its functional significance is debatable (Bewick et al., 2016; Bewick et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2020; Coleman-Derr and Zilberman, 2012; Le et al., 2020; Picard and Gehring, 2017; Shahzad et al., 2021; Takuno and Gaut, 2013; Wendte et al., 2019; Williams et al., 2021; Zilberman, 2017), it cannot be excluded that gbM is merely an evolutionary record of epigenetic collateral damage events that occurred in the past (Bewick and Schmitz, 2017; Bewick et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is speculative and supported by citations.

claim: Derepressed CMT3 and MET1 both prefer genic regions characterized by increased nucleosome stability.
source: Our results suggest that derepressed CMT3 and MET1 both prefer genic regions characterized by increased nucleosome stability (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is inferred from data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CMT3-induced CHG hypermethylation tends to occur away from transcription start and end sites of genes in a nearly identical pattern as observed for gbM.
source: Accordingly, CMT3-induced CHG hypermethylation tends to occur away from transcription start and end sites of genes in a nearly identical pattern as observed for gbM (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CHG methylation is more tolerated in central/3' biased regions because they are relatively inaccessible to trans-acting factors that regulate transcription.
source: We propose that CHG methylation is more tolerated in central/3' biased regions because they are relatively inaccessible to trans-acting factors that regulate transcription.
evidence: This claim is speculative.

claim: Genes that are consistently expressed can accumulate CHG methylation without having a large effect on steady state transcript levels and resulting fitness penalties, and thus be more likely to accumulate gbM over evolutionary time.
source: Perhaps genes that are consistently expressed can accumulate CHG methylation without having a large effect on steady state transcript levels and resulting fitness penalties, and thus be more likely to accumulate gbM over evolutionary time.
evidence: This claim is speculative.

claim: CMT3 off-targeting on genes may still occur despite complex regulatory mechanisms and the resulting epigenetic collateral damage can be recorded as heritable gbM.
source: However, CMT3 off-targeting on genes may still occur despite these complex regulatory mechanisms and the resulting epigenetic collateral damage can be recorded as heritable gbM.
evidence: This claim is speculative.

claim: The characteristic features of gbM may not pertain to its current functions, but rather the consequences of transient CHG methylation that occurred in the past and were selected on during evolution.
source: The characteristic features of gbM may not pertain to its current functions, but rather the consequences of transient CHG methylation that occurred in the past and were selected on during evolution.
evidence: This claim is speculative.
